exam.name: NCMHCE
exam.whyThisModuleMatters: This module gives learners a fast-reference glossary of high-yield counseling, diagnosis, ethics, assessment, trauma, group, research, and career terms likely to appear across NCMHCE case simulations and learning modules.

intro.summary: This glossary is designed as a fast-reference study tool. Instead of long lessons, it gives learners clean definitions, exam relevance, and related ideas that help them decode case vignettes faster.
learningObjectives: Recognize core counseling and diagnostic terms quickly
Differentiate similar concepts that are commonly confused on the exam
Use glossary terms to reinforce deeper module learning
Improve speed and confidence when reading clinical case language
howToUse: Use search when a term in a case vignette is unfamiliar.
Review related terms together when concepts are commonly confused.
Pair this glossary with the full theory, diagnosis, ethics, and crisis modules for deeper learning.

terms.definition: Emotional release that occurs when a person revisits a repressed or traumatic experience.
terms.examRelevance: May appear in trauma, psychodynamic, or emotionally intense processing contexts.

terms.definition: The process of adapting to a new culture while retaining, modifying, or losing aspects of the original culture.
terms.examRelevance: Useful in multicultural, developmental, immigrant, and family stress cases.

terms.definition: Trauma-related condition lasting from 3 days to 1 month after a traumatic event.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield differential from PTSD, which requires symptoms longer than 1 month.

terms.definition: How well a person manages everyday conceptual, social, and practical life demands.
terms.examRelevance: Important in intellectual disability and developmental assessment cases.

terms.definition: Fear and avoidance of situations where escape may be difficult or help unavailable if panic-like symptoms occur.
terms.examRelevance: Differentiate from panic disorder and specific phobia.

terms.definition: Medication side effect marked by inner restlessness and inability to sit still, often linked to antipsychotics.
terms.examRelevance: Common psychopharmacology test point under EPS.

terms.definition: Irvin Yalom therapeutic factor in which group members benefit from helping each other.
terms.examRelevance: Often tested in group scenarios.

terms.definition: Simultaneous conflicting feelings or motivations about a decision or behavior.
terms.examRelevance: Core concept in Motivational Interviewing and substance use cases.

terms.definition: Markedly reduced ability to feel pleasure or interest in previously enjoyable activities.
terms.examRelevance: Core symptom of Major Depressive Disorder.

terms.definition: Attachment pattern marked by fear of abandonment, clinginess, and hyperactivation of closeness needs.
terms.examRelevance: Relevant in trauma, couples, and personality-related cases.

terms.definition: Jean Piaget concept describing how new information is fitted into existing mental schemas.
terms.examRelevance: Appears in human development questions.

terms.definition: Ethical principle emphasizing the client's right to self-determination and informed decision-making.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield in informed consent and treatment choice scenarios.

terms.definition: Attachment pattern marked by suppression of closeness needs and discomfort with dependence or intimacy.
terms.examRelevance: Relevant in adult relationship and trauma conceptualization.

terms.definition: A structured CBT/behavioral intervention that increases planned, meaningful, mastery-building, or pleasurable activity to counter depression, withdrawal, and avoidance. It includes activity/mood monitoring, scheduling, barrier planning, and review rather than vague encouragement.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield for depression narratives with anhedonia, isolation, low motivation, disrupted routines, or avoidance. A strong exam answer is specific, collaborative, measurable, and tied to mood/functioning.

terms.definition: Ethical principle requiring action in the client's best interest.
terms.examRelevance: Common in ethics balancing questions.

terms.definition: Framework that explains mental health through interacting biological, psychological, and social factors.
terms.examRelevance: Central to case conceptualization and intake formulation.

terms.definition: The FDA's strongest medication warning, often highlighted for antidepressant-related suicidality risk in youth and young adults.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield psychopharmacology point.

terms.definition: Group leader intervention that stops harmful or unproductive member behavior.
terms.examRelevance: Frequently tested in group safety and scapegoating scenarios.

terms.definition: Professional limits that define and protect the therapeutic relationship.
terms.examRelevance: Major ethics topic in dual relationship and role confusion cases.

terms.definition: Intentional counselor effort to bring up race, culture, or identity factors that may affect the counseling relationship.
terms.examRelevance: Relevant in multicultural and alliance-building questions.

terms.definition: Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale, a structured tool for assessing suicidal ideation and behavior.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield suicide risk assessment tool.

terms.definition: Brief alcohol screening tool: Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield assessment tool for alcohol use screening.

terms.definition: Emotional release that brings relief or insight, especially in group work.
terms.examRelevance: Irvin Yalom therapeutic factor and trauma/group-related concept.

terms.definition: DBT strategy that maps the sequence of events, thoughts, emotions, and actions leading to a problem behavior.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield DBT intervention for self-harm and impulsive behavior cases.

terms.definition: Linda Gottfredson concept describing how children narrow career options over time based on role expectations, prestige, and interests.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield in career development.

terms.definition: Oversight of a counselor's work by a more experienced clinician to support competence, ethics, and client welfare.
terms.examRelevance: Important in ethics, supervision, and training questions.

terms.definition: ACT skill of seeing thoughts as mental events rather than literal truths.
terms.examRelevance: Differentiates ACT from CBT cognitive restructuring.

terms.definition: Inaccurate or unhelpful pattern of thinking such as catastrophizing or all-or-nothing thinking.
terms.examRelevance: Core CBT concept and a common exam clue in client statements.

terms.definition: Beck's depression model involving negative views of self, world, and future.
terms.examRelevance: Classic depression/CBT concept.

terms.definition: Sense of belonging, trust, and acceptance within a therapy group.
terms.examRelevance: One of the most important healing conditions in groups.

terms.definition: Information from sources other than the client, such as family, records, or other providers.
terms.examRelevance: Important in assessment, risk, and family-related cases.

terms.definition: Presence of two or more diagnosable conditions at the same time.
terms.examRelevance: Very common in diagnosis and case conceptualization.

terms.definition: Emotional exhaustion related to repeated exposure to others' suffering.
terms.examRelevance: Relevant to counselor impairment and trauma work.

terms.definition: Carl Rogers' term for genuineness and alignment between inner experience and outward expression.
terms.examRelevance: Core person-centered therapy condition.

terms.definition: A behavioral intervention that links clearly defined target behaviors to predictable reinforcers or consequences. In substance use care, incentives may be provided for negative drug screens, attendance, medication adherence, or other recovery behaviors.
terms.examRelevance: Often appears in substance use, school, residential, and structured treatment settings. Look for clear target behaviors, immediate feedback, consistency, and ethical reinforcement.

terms.definition: Counselor emotional reactions to the client that may be shaped by the counselor's own unresolved material.
terms.examRelevance: Important in psychodynamic and supervision questions.

terms.definition: Progress note format consisting of Data, Assessment, and Plan.
terms.examRelevance: Documentation format often contrasted with SOAP.

terms.definition: Experience of feeling detached from oneself, as if observing from outside the body or mind.
terms.examRelevance: Relevant in trauma, dissociation, and PTSD specifier cases.

terms.definition: Experience of feeling that surroundings are unreal, distant, or dreamlike.
terms.examRelevance: Relevant in trauma and dissociative presentations.

terms.definition: Murray Bowen family systems concept describing the ability to stay emotionally connected while maintaining a clear independent sense of self.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield family systems concept.

terms.definition: Attachment pattern marked by inconsistent or fearful responses, often linked to trauma or frightening caregiving.
terms.examRelevance: Relevant in trauma, attachment, and personality-related cases.

terms.definition: Disruption in normal integration of consciousness, memory, perception, or identity.
terms.examRelevance: Important in trauma, ASD, PTSD, and grounding/stabilization questions.

terms.definition: A second role with a client beyond counseling, such as friend, employer, teacher, or romantic partner.
terms.examRelevance: Major ethics concept in boundary and conflict-of-interest cases.

terms.definition: Legal and ethical obligation to take protective action when a client poses a serious threat to an identifiable third party.
terms.examRelevance: Very high-yield ethics/crisis concept.

terms.definition: Adlerian assessment tool using earliest memories to reveal lifestyle patterns and beliefs.
terms.examRelevance: Common Adlerian exam clue.

terms.definition: Statistic that shows the practical magnitude of a treatment effect or relationship.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield in research/program evaluation interpretation.

terms.definition: Thoughts, urges, or behaviors that feel unwanted and inconsistent with the self.
terms.examRelevance: Classic clue for OCD-related symptoms.

terms.definition: Thoughts, traits, or behaviors experienced as natural, justified, or consistent with the self.
terms.examRelevance: Useful in personality disorder and OCPD differentials.

terms.definition: Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing, an evidence-based trauma treatment using bilateral stimulation during trauma processing.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield PTSD treatment model.

terms.definition: Accurately understanding and communicating understanding of the client's inner world.
terms.examRelevance: Core Carl Rogers person-centered condition and broadly central counseling skill.

terms.definition: Helping clients recognize and use their strengths, agency, and capacity for change.
terms.examRelevance: Relevant in trauma-informed care, multicultural work, and person-centered approaches.

terms.definition: Structural family therapy concept describing overly diffuse boundaries and excessive involvement among family members.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield family systems term.

terms.definition: Systems concept that different paths can lead to the same outcome.
terms.examRelevance: Useful in family systems and case conceptualization reasoning.

terms.definition: Exposure and Response Prevention, an evidence-based OCD treatment involving exposure to feared stimuli while resisting compulsive rituals.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield OCD treatment term.

terms.definition: Irvin Yalom therapeutic factor involving confrontation with freedom, responsibility, mortality, isolation, and meaning.
terms.examRelevance: Common group theory term.

terms.definition: Narrative therapy practice of separating the problem from the person.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield narrative therapy clue.

terms.definition: A behavioral process in which the reinforcement maintaining a behavior is withheld so the behavior gradually decreases. An extinction burst may occur first, meaning the behavior temporarily intensifies before improving.
terms.examRelevance: Commonly tested in behavior plans. The exam may ask whether escalation after withdrawing reinforcement means the plan failed; often it is an extinction burst requiring consistency and reinforcement of replacement behavior.

terms.definition: Federal law protecting educational records from unauthorized disclosure.
terms.examRelevance: Important in school counseling and educational settings.

terms.definition: Adlerian concept describing imagined goals or ideals that guide behavior.
terms.examRelevance: Common Adlerian conceptual clue in perfectionism and self-worth cases.

terms.definition: Ethical principle of trustworthiness, keeping commitments, and maintaining professional reliability.
terms.examRelevance: Relevant in alliance, documentation, supervision, and boundaries.

terms.definition: Gottman predictors of relationship breakdown: criticism, contempt, defensiveness, and stonewalling.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield couples counseling concept.

terms.definition: Behavioral assessment method that identifies antecedents, behaviors, and consequences to determine the function of a behavior.
terms.examRelevance: Important in child, school, and behavior planning cases.

terms.definition: Brief self-report measure of generalized anxiety severity.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield assessment tool for anxiety screening and monitoring.

terms.definition: Adlerian concept often translated as social interest or community feeling.
terms.examRelevance: Key marker of Adlerian mental health.

terms.definition: Diagram of family relationships and patterns across generations.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield family systems assessment tool.

terms.definition: Experiential therapy emphasizing present-moment awareness, unfinished business, and direct contact with experience.
terms.examRelevance: Often signaled by empty-chair or here-and-now work.

terms.definition: Strong sense of group belonging, trust, and emotional connection.
terms.examRelevance: Critical group healing factor and common exam concept.

terms.definition: Federal law governing privacy and protection of health information in covered healthcare settings.
terms.examRelevance: Essential ethics/legal term.

terms.definition: RIASEC career typology: Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, Conventional.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield career counseling framework.

terms.definition: Thoughts of killing or seriously harming another person.
terms.examRelevance: Important in violence risk and duty-to-protect questions.

terms.definition: Excessive sleepiness or sleeping for unusually long periods.
terms.examRelevance: Possible symptom of depression and atypical presentations.

terms.definition: Elevated or irritable mood with increased energy lasting at least 4 days, less severe than mania and without marked impairment or psychosis.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield differential point for Bipolar II vs MDD.

terms.definition: Internal Family Systems model viewing the mind as composed of parts led by a core Self.
terms.examRelevance: Theory clue when cases use part language and inner conflict.

terms.definition: Counselor skill of addressing what is happening in the therapeutic relationship in the present moment.
terms.examRelevance: Relevant in person-centered, process, and group interventions.

terms.definition: Ongoing process of explaining counseling, risks, benefits, limits, and client rights so the client can make an informed choice.
terms.examRelevance: One of the most heavily tested ethics concepts.

terms.definition: Irvin Yalom therapeutic factor in which members gain hope by seeing that improvement is possible.
terms.examRelevance: Common group therapy exam clue.

terms.definition: Framework recognizing that multiple social identities and systems of oppression/privilege interact.
terms.examRelevance: Relevant in multicultural, trauma, and social justice-informed cases.

terms.definition: Ethical principle of fairness and equitable treatment.
terms.examRelevance: Important in ethics, nondiscrimination, and access-related questions.

terms.definition: Career theorist John Krumboltz, known for social learning theory of career development and planned happenstance.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield career counseling theory.

terms.definition: Clinical evaluation of the likelihood that a suicidal or violent thought may be acted upon.
terms.examRelevance: Core part of crisis and safety work.

terms.definition: Intensity and setting of treatment appropriate to a client's needs, such as outpatient, IOP, PHP, residential, or inpatient.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield in crisis, substance use, psychosis, and severity decisions.

terms.definition: Adlerian term for an individual's characteristic pattern of beliefs, goals, and behavior formed early in life.
terms.examRelevance: Classic Adlerian conceptual term.

terms.definition: Group leader skill that connects themes or experiences across members.
terms.examRelevance: Frequently tested group intervention.

terms.definition: Professional who is legally required to report certain forms of abuse or neglect.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield legal/ethics concept.

terms.definition: Distinct period of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy lasting at least 1 week or requiring hospitalization.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield bipolar differential concept.

terms.definition: Arithmetic average of a set of scores.
terms.examRelevance: Basic research/statistics term.

terms.definition: Urie Bronfenbrenner ecological systems level involving the person's immediate environment, such as family, school, and peers.
terms.examRelevance: Key in child and systems-based cases.

terms.definition: SFBT question inviting the client to imagine how life would look if the problem were solved.
terms.examRelevance: Classic solution-focused clue.

terms.definition: Collaborative, person-centered method for exploring and resolving ambivalence about change.
terms.examRelevance: Very high-yield in substance use and behavior change cases.

terms.definition: Mental Status Examination, a structured assessment of current mental functioning.
terms.examRelevance: Essential in assessment and case conceptualization.

terms.definition: Approach emphasizing cultural humility, openness, and responsiveness in the counseling relationship.
terms.examRelevance: Relevant in multicultural and alliance questions.

terms.definition: Removing something desirable after a behavior to decrease that behavior, such as loss of privileges after repeated rule-breaking.

terms.definition: Removing or escaping something unpleasant after a behavior, which increases that behavior. Avoidance that reduces anxiety is a classic example.

terms.definition: Schizophrenia-related deficits such as flat affect, avolition, alogia, anhedonia, and asociality.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield psychosis differential concept.

terms.definition: Chemical messenger that transmits signals between neurons.
terms.examRelevance: Basic psychopharmacology knowledge point.

terms.definition: Cross's model of Black racial identity development.
terms.examRelevance: Relevant in multicultural and identity development questions.

terms.definition: Ethical principle of avoiding harm.
terms.examRelevance: Major ethics principle in safety and boundary decisions.

terms.definition: Research assumption that there is no meaningful difference or relationship.
terms.examRelevance: Basic research concept.

terms.definition: Core MI skills: Open-ended questions, Affirmations, Reflective listening, Summaries.
terms.examRelevance: Classic Motivational Interviewing exam concept.

terms.definition: Jean Piaget concept that objects continue to exist even when out of sight.
terms.examRelevance: Human development concept in early childhood.

terms.definition: Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder, an ego-syntonic pattern of perfectionism, rigidity, and control.

terms.definition: Learning in which behavior is shaped by consequences, including reinforcement, punishment, extinction, and shaping.

terms.definition: PTSD Checklist for DSM-5, a self-report measure of PTSD symptoms.

terms.definition: Nine-item self-report tool for depression severity screening and monitoring.

terms.definition: Adding an unpleasant consequence after a behavior to decrease that behavior, such as a brief corrective consequence after aggression.

terms.definition: Added psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech, and disorganized behavior.

terms.definition: Legal protection that may prevent a counselor from being forced to testify about client disclosures without consent, depending on jurisdiction.

terms.definition: Assessment using ambiguous stimuli to elicit themes or unconscious material, such as the Rorschach or TAT.

terms.definition: Providing information to help clients understand symptoms, treatment, coping, or diagnoses.
terms.examRelevance: Common intervention across many theories and settings.

terms.definition: Noticeable slowing of speech, movement, and mental activity.

terms.definition: DBT skill of fully accepting reality as it is, without approving of it or giving up on change.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield DBT concept.

terms.definition: Offering an alternative, more useful way of understanding a situation or behavior.

terms.definition: Planning for high-risk situations, triggers, and coping responses to reduce return to problematic behavior.

terms.definition: Signed authorization that allows the counselor to share specified information with a specified person or organization.
terms.examRelevance: Important in ethics, collaboration, and records questions.

terms.definition: Capacity to adapt or recover in the face of adversity.

terms.definition: John Holland's six career interest/environment types: Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, Conventional.

terms.definition: Collaborative written plan identifying warning signs, coping strategies, supports, crisis resources, means restriction, and reasons for living.

terms.definition: Lev Vygotsky concept involving temporary support from a more knowledgeable other to help learning occur.

terms.definition: SFBT questions that ask clients to rate progress, motivation, or distress on a numerical scale.

terms.definition: Trauma-like symptoms that develop from indirect exposure to other people's traumatic experiences.
terms.examRelevance: Relevant in counselor impairment and trauma work.

terms.definition: Carl Rogers' concept of the natural drive toward growth, fulfillment, and becoming more fully oneself.

terms.definition: Reinforcing successive approximations toward a target behavior rather than waiting for the final behavior to occur perfectly.
terms.examRelevance: Useful when the final goal is too difficult at first, such as school attendance, group participation, exposure steps, communication skills, hygiene routines, or social skills.

terms.definition: Goals that are Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Realistic, and Timely.

terms.definition: Progress note format consisting of Subjective, Objective, Assessment, and Plan.

terms.definition: Adlerian sense of connection to humanity and contribution to others; a marker of mental health.
terms.examRelevance: Key Adlerian concept.

terms.definition: CBT technique of using guided questions to examine assumptions and develop more balanced thinking.

terms.definition: Model of behavior change: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance, and relapse.

terms.definition: Approach focusing on client abilities, resilience, and resources rather than only deficits.
terms.examRelevance: Useful across case conceptualization and treatment planning.

terms.definition: Minuchin's family therapy model focused on boundaries, hierarchy, subsystems, and family organization.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield family therapy theory.

terms.definition: Thoughts about suicide, ranging from passive wishes for death to active plans and intent.
terms.examRelevance: One of the most heavily tested crisis topics.

terms.definition: Career theorist Donald Super, who described lifespan career development and the implementation of self-concept across life roles.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield career counseling theory.

terms.definition: Potentially irreversible involuntary repetitive movements, often caused by long-term antipsychotic use.
terms.examRelevance: Major psychopharmacology safety concept.

terms.definition: Planned therapeutic ending of the counseling relationship.
terms.examRelevance: Important in treatment planning, ethics, and continuity-of-care questions.

terms.definition: Collaborative, trusting working relationship between counselor and client.
terms.examRelevance: One of the strongest predictors of outcome and central across all theories.

terms.definition: CBT worksheet or strategy for identifying situations, thoughts, feelings, evidence, and alternative interpretations.
terms.examRelevance: Classic CBT tool.

terms.definition: A structured reinforcement system in which tokens, points, or credits are earned for defined target behaviors and exchanged for meaningful rewards or privileges.
terms.examRelevance: Often appears in school, inpatient, residential, child/adolescent, group, or skills-training settings. Strong answers specify target behaviors, exchange rules, consistency, and ethical safeguards.

terms.definition: Client's unconscious redirection of feelings and expectations from past relationships onto the counselor.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield psychodynamic concept.

terms.definition: Approach that recognizes trauma's impact and emphasizes safety, trust, collaboration, empowerment, and cultural responsiveness.
terms.examRelevance: Very high-yield trauma framework.

terms.definition: Collaborative clinical plan outlining diagnosis, goals, objectives, interventions, strengths, barriers, and level of care.
terms.examRelevance: Core case conceptualization and documentation concept.

terms.definition: Murray Bowen family systems concept in which tension between two people is stabilized by involving a third person.
terms.examRelevance: Very high-yield family systems clue.

terms.definition: Group development stages: forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning.

terms.definition: Carl Rogers' principle of accepting the client without judgment or conditions of worth.
terms.examRelevance: Core person-centered therapy condition.

terms.definition: Irvin Yalom therapeutic factor involving the realization that one is not alone in one's struggles.
terms.examRelevance: Classic group counseling test point.

terms.definition: Degree to which a test or study measures what it claims to measure.
terms.examRelevance: Core research and assessment concept.

terms.definition: Personally meaningful directions or principles that guide action, especially in ACT.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield ACT concept.

terms.definition: Cumulative transformation of the helper's worldview through repeated empathic exposure to trauma survivors.
terms.examRelevance: Relevant in trauma work, ethics, and supervision.

terms.definition: Reality Therapy sequence: Wants, Doing, Evaluation, Planning.
terms.examRelevance: Classic Reality Therapy clue.

terms.definition: Optimal arousal zone in which a person can remain regulated enough to think, feel, and process effectively.
terms.examRelevance: High-yield trauma and stabilization concept.

terms.definition: DBT concept describing the integration of emotional mind and rational mind.
terms.examRelevance: Common DBT clue in emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness cases.

terms.definition: Group theorist known for identifying 11 therapeutic factors and for existential group psychotherapy.
terms.examRelevance: Essential group counseling name and framework.

terms.definition: Lev Vygotsky concept describing what a learner can do with guidance but not yet independently.
terms.examRelevance: Important development and learning term.

commonConfusions.title: Ego-Dystonic vs Ego-Syntonic
commonConfusions.difference: Ego-dystonic symptoms feel unwanted and foreign, while ego-syntonic traits feel natural or acceptable to the person.

commonConfusions.title: Universality vs Group Cohesion
commonConfusions.difference: Universality is realizing others share the same struggle; group cohesion is the bond and trust within the group.

commonConfusions.title: Mandated Reporting vs Duty to Warn / Protect
commonConfusions.difference: Mandated reporting usually concerns abuse/neglect duties; duty to protect concerns serious danger to self or identifiable others.

commonConfusions.title: PTSD vs Acute Stress Disorder
commonConfusions.difference: ASD occurs from 3 days to 1 month after trauma; PTSD requires symptoms lasting longer than 1 month.

commonConfusions.title: OCD vs OCPD
commonConfusions.difference: OCD involves ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions; OCPD is an ego-syntonic personality style of perfectionism and control.

finalTakeaways: This glossary is best used as a fast-reference layer, not a replacement for the full modules.
When a term appears in a case, ask what decision it should trigger clinically.
The more quickly learners can decode the language of a vignette, the more likely they are to pick the best next step.
